title: Perception: the eyes, the HUD and her own state
tagline: Pixels in; her place, vitals, minimap and the screen's checks out, no map knowledge.
summary: The core of the perception layer: Eyes, the only door to the game's pixels, turns each checked frame into an Observation (her name tag, HP/MP, the ground and ropes, minimap dots, her EXP/HP/level boxes) in screen pixels. Around it sit the frame source and frame checks, exact readers for the HUD's numbers and her heading, the plate and pose cues her scene-based place uses, readers for the stat and key bindings windows, and the matching helpers the monster and loot detectors share.
details_md:
### Where this slice sits

The autonomous player (`gamelab`) is layered like a self-driving stack; perception is the bottom layer. It imports no other gamelab layer, only gamelab's shared modules: `tests/test_architecture.py` enforces that, its shared set being `capture`, `character`, `classes`, `directions`, `gcstats`, `native`, `paths`, `screen`, `telemetry` and `window` (the package docstring still names the first five it had; this slice also uses `native` for its C and `directions`). Outside gamelab it uses `gamedata` for the game's own pictures and `maplehelper` for OCR. The same test holds the one-capture rule: only localization/service.py makes `ScreenFrames`, and only frames.py calls `capture.shared()`. It knows nothing of the map: everything it says is in screen pixels, and localization turns that into map units.

### One process looks

Since 2026-10-25 the game is captured by one process only, the **perception service** (`python -m gamelab perceive`, localization/service.py). Its frame loop takes a `Frame` from `ScreenFrames` (frames.py) 15 times a second through the process's single DXGI desktop duplication (mss as fallback), never bringing the game forward, and hands it to `Eyes.look_at` (eyes.py), which builds an `Observation`. Commands (a hunt, the pet, `hunt look`) read the service's states over a pipe; their own Eyes have `NoScreen`, which refuses to capture.

### Checked before read

A frame is read only if it really is the game as expected (framecheck.py): the window there, in front, uncovered, the right client size, not moved during the shot, the frame fresh, and two anchors the game draws at fixed pixels (the minimap's title strip and the HUD's border on row 700) in place. A failure is a `Problem` whose *kind* decides the response: reopen the capture (offset, stale, capture), wait for the user (size, minimized, gone, offscreen), or Alt+Enter twice from a command that acts (size, drawn). The checks came after 2026-10-24, when a hunt read her place off the map and sent a plan off a rope every 5 s for two minutes, a window drag produced offset frames, and another program's window was captured.

### What an Observation holds

- **Her on screen**: her name tag's centre (nametag.py: gray template matching near where she was), or through the scene `locator` that localization supplies, her plate's exact colours (plate.py) or her body against her own pose bank (poses.py), with her feet.
- **Her vitals**: HP and MP fractions from bar colours (hud.py), and boxes for the exact glyph-by-glyph readers of her EXP number, HP number and level (exp_number.py, hp_number.py, lv_number.py), which the world step runs only when their pixels change.
- **The minimap**: her yellow dot and other players' markers (minimap.py), shifted by where the map's own minimap picture sits so they always read with one origin.
- **Terrain**: the ground under her and ropes in view (terrain.py).

Further questions about a look's frame go through Eyes methods: monsters, re-finds, drops, a monster's HP bar (hud.py), her facing (heading.py). The simulator's `FakeEyes` subclasses Eyes and answers the same questions from its world, which is why localization never reads pixels itself.

### Three pixel spaces

**Full-size px** are the client area's own pixels (minimap dots, ropes, the bar boxes). **Look-frame px** are the client shrunk `look_scale` times: half size on the old 1920x1080 window, full size at the game's own 1366x768, which it has run at since 2026-10-23 (her tag, the ground, monsters). **Game px** are the game's own 1366x768 picture, one per map unit (glyph positions, the HUD's anchors). `screen.Geometry` converts the many constants measured on the 1920x1080 window to any size.

### Exactness over thresholds

At its own size the game draws its pictures pixel for pixel, and several readers exploit that. The number readers draw every glyph at every position and find the best path by dynamic programming, refusing any reading whose cells don't clearly fit: a wrong value must never come out, no value is fine. The plate (plate.py) and the exact finder (exact.py) count exact colours, so whatever covers part of her or a monster only removes evidence. The KEY BINDINGS and stat windows are matched against the game copy's own UI pictures. The price: these readers need lossless frames at 1366x768 (JPEG recordings fail them by design).

### Helpers and windows

match.py is the masked colour match (in C with AVX2, about four times OpenCV's speed) used by the monster and loot detectors; sprites.py builds monster templates from the game's sprites and makes the map's detector; gates.py learns which colours belong to a monster kind; kinds.py names kinds. stat_window.py reads her stat window (W.DEF for the safety stop) and keybindings.py the KEY BINDINGS window (which key ATTACK is on); behavior opens and closes those windows, perception only reads frames.

modules.title: Eyes
modules.tagline: Perception's only door to pixels: a frame becomes an Observation.
modules.summary: `Eyes` reads a game window of one client size (a `screen.Geometry`). `look_at` turns a full-size RGB frame into an `Observation` (her tag, HP/MP, the ground, minimap dots, ropes, the boxes her EXP, HP and level are read from); `look` captures one first. Localization then asks Eyes questions about the look's frame (monsters, re-finds, drops, a monster's HP bar, her heading) instead of reading pixels itself, so the simulator's FakeEyes can stand in for the game by answering the same questions.
modules.details_md:
**What a look is.** `Eyes.look_at(full, t, ropes)` takes one full-size RGB picture of the game's client area (exactly `geo.client`, else `ValueError`) and builds an `Observation`, in this order:

1. HP and MP from the bar colours (`hud.bars`) and the chat box's state (`chatbox.read`, 35-80 us), read even on a frame that fails its checks: both are the UI's own pixels.
2. The look frame: the picture shrunk `geo.look_scale` times with `INTER_AREA` (half size at the old 1920x1080 window; at the game's own 1366x768 the look frame *is* the full picture).
3. The frame checks (`framecheck.frame_problem`, 0.04 ms on a good frame). A failure returns a *refused* Observation: `bad` set, no tag, and the last good frame's HP and MP (a frame off the client area read 0% HP at 16:48:45, which looked like a hit).
4. The map's own minimap picture found in the minimap window (`MinimapPicture.find`). Never found means her dot's origin is unknown: refused as kind `picture`.
5. Her yellow dot (`minimap.her_dot`), searched only up to 2 px past the picture's right edge (on Ellinia, 2026-10-29, a house's yellow trim beside the minimap was taken for her dot), and other players' markers (0.4-0.6 ms); both shifted as if the picture sat where it did on the first map (`MinimapPicture.shift`).
6. Her place on screen: the `locator` (localization's scene-based `Locator`, using `plate` and `poses`) when Senses gave one, else `NameTag.find`. A `RuntimeError` (her full-size tag template can't be cut: she isn't on screen) refuses the look as kind `tag`; any other exception from the locator turns it off for good and is logged.
7. The ground under her (`terrain.ground_extent`, from the row `TAG_BELOW_FEET` above her tag, or her feet's row from the locator) and, when `want_ropes` is on (Senses turns it on), ropes in the x ranges Senses asks for (`rope_columns`).
8. The bottom bar: her EXP number's text pixels (any channel over `EXP_TEXT`, 150) and copies of the EXP, HP and level boxes, which the glyph readers read later, only when the pixels change.

**Capturing.** Only eyes with a screen capture. `look()` calls `_capture()`: `window_wait()` first (a window of another size, minimized, gone or off screen is waited out without capturing or bringing the game forward: the reviewer's focus.py had a hunt pull the game over the user's work 136 times in 63 s), then the game brought to the front if it isn't (0.3 s pause), the client rect read, the window checked (`framecheck.window_problem`), a shot shown after the look began, the rect read again (`moved_problem`) and the shot's age checked (`stale_problem`). A window that moved between two good looks is logged and sent as a telemetry `window` event. `glance()` takes just the minimap box, one HP row and the minimap's title strip from the newest frame, no sooner than `GLANCE_EVERY_S` (63 ms) after the last glance began: her dot and HP for watching a plan run.

**Recovering.** `recover(problem)` makes the minimap picture, the name tag and the locator search afresh. When the capture itself may be at fault (`framecheck.CAPTURE_KINDS`: offset, stale, capture) it reopens the DXGI duplication at the first such failure, has mss take over for `capture.RETRY_S` (10 s) at the second, then the two in turn every `CAPTURE_AGAIN_S` (5 s). It never moves or resizes the window.

**Questions about a look.** `monsters` (a band of rows from map units above to below her feet, `band_rows`), `monsters_wide`, `refind` / `refind_all` / `refind_ahead` (tracked monsters looked for again: in C on threads, or sent to the GPU ahead of the look at 1366x768 only), `items` / `items_in` (a `LootDetector` made on first use for the map's `drop_names`), `bar` (a monster's HP bar, `hud.hp_bar`), `misses` (her MISS popups), `heading` / `learn_heading` / `keep_heading` (her facing, through a `Heading` made on first use). `sim.fakes.FakeEyes` subclasses Eyes and answers these from the simulated world.

**No screen for commands.** A command's eyes get `NoScreen`, whose `shot` raises: only the perception service captures (a third DXGI duplication failed with 0x887A0022 when `watch`, the pet's babysitter and a hunt each held one). What a command reads off a whole frame (`messages`: the pickup log by OCR, about 0.4 s; `chat_line`: the message bar's game line) comes from the service's full frame (`full_frames`).

modules.title: Frames for the perception service
modules.tagline: The game window as the screen shows it, checked, never brought forward.
modules.summary: `ScreenFrames.next(after)` gives the perception service's frame loop one `Frame` a pass through the process's single grabber (DXGI desktop duplication, or mss). Unfit frames come back marked not visible with a `framecheck.Problem` instead of raising; stalled frames keep their own time; pictures are reused to save memory faults. `ListFrames` plays saved frames back, and `glimpse` grabs the client at any size for the Lie Detector and HUD checks.
modules.details_md:
**`ScreenFrames.next(after)`** is called by the perception service's frame loop (`localization.feed.run`) once a pass (15 a second since 2026-10-30). It never brings the game forward: a capture sees whatever is on top, so every frame is checked.

1. *The window* (`framecheck.window_problem`): gone, minimized, another client size, partly off screen, not in front, or covered at a 7 x 5 grid of points. Any of these returns `Frame.unfit` (`visible` False, `full` None, a Problem saying why) and the loop waits for the game to come back.
2. *The shot*: `grabber.shot(area, after=after)` waits for a frame shown at `after` or later (DXGI waits up to 20 ms, `capture.FRESH_WAIT_S`) and the crop is converted BGRA to RGB straight into one of the kept `Pictures`. A capture that throws (mss refused, a duplication that can't be made, a full-screen switch) is kind `capture`: the loop goes on, where it once ended the service.
3. *After the shot*: the client rect read again (`moved_problem`: a window being dragged moves between two reads), the frame's age (`stale_problem`, 2 s), and the game drawing off its client area (`drawn_problem`, given the window frame's inset, which only this module knows).
4. *Its time.* A frame shown within `HELD_S` (0.5 s) before `after` is stamped *now* (the screen hadn't changed); those held 50-500 ms (`HELD_COUNT_S`) are counted for the service's 10 s console line (`holds`). A frame held longer is a stall: it keeps its own present time and a `held` event is said once until fresh frames come (live on 2026-10-26 a hunt stood still on a 2.1 s old frame, and before that frames up to 2 s old had been stamped as now and acted on).
5. `new` is False when the present time equals the last frame's: the feed skips its world step for an unchanged screen nobody asked about.

**`Pictures`** keeps up to `PICTURES` (24) RGB buffers and converts each frame into one nobody else holds (its reference count is the list's alone, `sys.getrefcount`), so a frame handed out to the step, a search, the recording or a client is never overwritten. A new 1366x768 picture each frame was 3 MB and 770 page faults that Windows' kernel zeroes (23,000 a second at 30 frames); reuse took the replay from 39,700 faults a second to 28,800.

**Windows over the game.** With `cover_check` on (only while the service's rolling recording runs) `cover()` walks the z-order above the game before and after the shot and names the nearest other program's window over the client (`Frame.over`) with the boxes they cover (`over_boxes`). The walk calls user32 through `ctypes.PyDLL`, keeping Python's lock (none of those calls sends a message): two walks a frame went from 1.75 ms to 1.2 ms; with the game in front only the topmost windows are above it (44 on this PC, 0.077 ms). Perception reads such a frame as usual. Since 2026-11-01 the rolling recording keeps it as it is with the covered boxes noted; a frame covered over all of the game, or whose boxes aren't known, is a gap ("covered") in the recording.

**`glimpse(title)`** grabs the client at any size, unchecked, 1366x768 and 1920x1080 as they are and any other size brought to 1920x1080 (`lie_detector.to_template`): the service answers `full` asks with it while its frames aren't fit for a fault Alt+Enter mends, so the size fix can look for the Lie Detector first and the pet for the HUD. A 3840x2160 picture takes 12 ms to convert and shrink.

**`ListFrames`** hands saved frames over in turn, round and round, each stamped when handed over: tests and offline soaks of the feed.

modules.title: Frame checks
modules.tagline: Is this capture really the game, where and as the eyes expect?
modules.summary: Decides whether a capture may be read: the window (minimized, size, on screen, in front, uncovered), whether it moved during the shot, whether the frame is stale, and two anchors the game draws at fixed pixels at 1366x768 (the minimap's title strip and the HUD's border). A failure is a `Problem` whose kind tells Eyes.recover and the commands what to do; `BadLook` and `LookLost` carry it as exceptions.
modules.details_md:
Two **anchors**, which the game draws at the same pixels on every map at its own 1366x768, tell whether a frame lines up with the client area:

- the minimap window's title strip ("MINI MAP", `TITLE_BOX` x 0-80, rows 2-20) against `assets/minimap_title.png`: mean absolute difference at most `TITLE_DIFF` (10). On 79 good frames 0.0-1.1; shifted 1 px 24-33 (the README says 22-33, which counts a 2 px shift across); another window over the game 191. A server notice's dark band halves the strip's brightness, so it is also compared with the picture at half brightness (`TITLE_DIMMED_DIFF`, 5: 0.46 under the notice of 2026-11-05 18:31:42);
- the HUD's border: row 700 (`screen.HUD_TOP_GAME`) darker than `HUD_DARK` (40) in every channel and row 701 brighter than `HUD_WHITE` (200), sampled every 4th px of x 290-1075, at least half of them (`HUD_SHARE`), and the white row's ends at x 285 and 1080 (`ends_right`), which tell a shift across.

**`frame_problem`** (0.04 ms on a good frame) fails a frame as `minimap` or `hud`. When both anchors are off it searches the border 48 px each way (`find_offset`, about 4 ms, only then) to say how far the frame is `offset` (the frames of the 16:48 drag came out +26,+26 and -5,+6). If instead the border is whole much further up (`_far`: up to `DRAWN_REACH` 160 px, `DRAWN_ACROSS` 64 across) the game itself drew its picture off its client: kind `drawn` (seen 2026-10-25 23:40 at (-18, -85); Alt+Enter twice set it right). `ScreenFrames` knows the window frame's inset and also catches a drawn picture nearer than 48 px exactly there (`drawn_offset`, within `DRAWN_SLACK` 2).

**`window_problem`** (about 0.25 ms) checks the window itself, the faults the user sets right first: minimized, a client of another size, partly off every monitor, not in front, or another window over it at a grid of points (`COVER_GRID` (6, 4) spaces, 7 x 5 points 225 x 188 px apart at 1366x768: the five points used before missed a box over x 300-660, y 60-360). `moved_problem` and `stale_problem` (`STALE_S`, 2 s) cover the capture itself.

**Kinds decide what happens next.**

| Group | Kinds | Response |
|---|---|---|
| `CAPTURE_KINDS` | offset, stale, capture | the capture may be at fault: Eyes.recover reopens the duplication or falls back to mss |
| `WAIT_KINDS` | size, minimized, gone, offscreen | only the user sets these right: a look asks the window alone and never brings the game forward |
| `FIX_KINDS` | size, drawn | Alt+Enter twice mends them (control.window_size, from a command that acts) |
| others | window, moved, minimap, hud, picture, tag, place | taken again shortly; `place` is localization.placecheck's |

`BadLook` carries a Problem as an exception (raised by `Eyes.look`); `LookLost` is raised by Senses after `LOST_S` (3 s) of failed looks, and nothing may act until a look passes.

**`hud_seen`** matches the HUD's three buttons (CASH SHOP, MENU, SHORT CUT) on a frame of any size brought to 1366x768: 0.774 or more on the good frames and as clients of 3840x2160, 2560x1440, 1600x900, 1396x1952, 1350x700 and 1280x720 show them (69 frames), 0.52 at most on the desktop or the play area moved over the HUD. It tells "the game is in play" where the 1-px border doesn't survive resampling (the size fix and the pet use it).

Nothing is checked at 1920x1080 or in the simulator (`checked(geo)`): the anchors were measured at 1366x768 only.

modules.title: Learned colour gates
modules.tagline: Which colours belong to a monster kind, learned against the map's background.
modules.summary: Step 1 of the monster search (mobs.py) matches a kind's silhouette only where the kind's colour is. The first map's four kinds have hand-made colour tests (mobs.PALETTES); every other kind gets a gate learned from data: a colour bin is the kind's when it is at least 5 times commoner in the kind's own pictures than in the map's background. All of a detector's learned gates are one lookup a pixel.
modules.details_md:
**Colour bins.** A colour is binned to `BITS` (5) bits a channel, 32,768 bins (`bins`, `index`: red highest). On West Rocky Mountain II's stumps at 1920x1080 half size, 4 bits made gates take 5.8% of the background for 69% of the stumps' colours, 6 bits 0.2% for 38%, 5 bits 1.8% for 61%.

**A kind's colours** (`kind_histograms`) are its templates' pixels as step 1 sees them (the game's sprites shrunk to step 1's scale, at either window size), as drawn and blended toward a fog's white (`FOG` (245, 245, 245), alphas `FOG_ALPHAS` 1.0, 0.7, 0.4): the masked match itself doesn't mind fog, only the gate did (red snails under West Rocky Mountain II's fog went from 48 to 53 of 57 found).

**The background's colours** (`background`) are the play area of saved frames of the map (above the HUD, at step 1's scale) with the monsters found on them cut out; `sprites.learn_background` measures them (`python -m gamelab learn-colours`) and `save_background` keeps the counts in `assets/backgrounds/<map id>.npz` (in git; the frames stay out).

**Learning** (`learn`). With half a pixel added to every bin (so a colour the background never shows is the kind's if its pictures have it at all, and one neither has isn't), a bin is the kind's where its share of any one blend's pixels is at least `RATIO` (5) times its share of the background's. Tree Dungeon's two kinds' gates take 0.98% and 1.22% of its background.

**One lookup** (`Gates`). Each colour bin's entry holds a bit per kind (uint8 up to 8 kinds, uint16 to 16, uint32 to 32), so step 1 computes each pixel's bin once and looks it up once whatever the number of kinds; `test` is called like a hand-made colour test on a picture's int16 channels. The exact finder (exact.py) also uses `bins` and the background counts to pick anchors on colours sparse on the map.

modules.title: Minimap dots
modules.tagline: Her yellow dot, other players' markers, and where the map's picture sits.
modules.summary: Finds her yellow dot and other players' coloured markers in the minimap window at the top left, in full-size px, and locates the map's own minimap picture in the window so the dots can be read with one origin even when the window centres or scrolls the picture.
modules.details_md:
Every dot is one of the game's own markers: hers a yellow core 6 game px across; others' a core 5 across in a dark grey ring and white halo (stranger red, party orange, guild lavender, buddy cyan). At 1366x768 each marker is its picture pixel for pixel; at 1920x1080 the whole picture is stretched 1.40625x with bilinear filtering.

**Her dot** (`her_dot`, `dot_in_box`). In the minimap box (`MINIMAP_BOX` (0, 95, 300, 300) at 1920x1080; (0, 68, 213, 213) at 1366x768) pixels with red over 220, green over 190 and blue under 90 are yellow. Connected blobs with an area in `DOT_AREA` (12-200 px at 1920x1080, scaled by area elsewhere) and neither side over `DOT_SIZE` (16) qualify, and the biggest is her dot (its centroid). A blob narrower or shorter than a full dot (`DOT_FULL` 7, never under `DOT_CORE` 6) with another player's marker touching it is partly covered, so its middle is taken from the side that shows (`_uncovered`, `DOT_UNCOVER`): a marker drawn 4-5 game px off pulled her yellow's middle 1.3-1.7 px its way on average; taken so, 0.4.

**Other players** (`other_dots`, `markers_in_box`). Each kind's core colour is an HSV range (`MARKER_COLOURS`); a kind is skipped where its colour isn't present at all (0.44 ms a look against 1.9 counting each kind's blobs over the whole box). A blob must be a core's size (`MARKER_AREA` 14-52 px, `MARKER_SIDE` 4-9), solid at 1366x768 (`MARKER_FILL` 0.7: a portal's inner ring passed as a buddy's core otherwise), and ringed by dark grey in at least 60% of 16 directions (`RING_DARK`, `_ringed`). Her yellow, the party leader's crown, NPC green and the minimap's dark blue are none of the kinds; the buddy range stops 2 hue steps short of other cyan markers that had been found as buddies. Two markers 5 game px apart or more (57 map units) are two; 4 px apart, a third of the time; nearer, the one drawn last hides most of the other's core and they read as one.

**The map's minimap picture** (`MinimapPicture`, from 2026-10-24). The window centres the map's picture under the map's name and, on a map taller than it shows (Tree Dungeon: 67 x 183 game px in a window showing 112 rows), scrolls the picture to keep her dot in view, so where a map point lands on screen moves as she climbs; read with the first map's origin, her x came out 902 on a map 360..410 wide. The picture (`mapdata.minimap_picture`, from the game data; resized by the stretch at 1920x1080) is matched in horizontal bands (`PICTURE_BAND`, 0.55 of the box's height) with `TM_CCOEFF_NORMED`: first within `PICTURE_NEAR` (16 px) of the last corner, then every quarter band over the whole box. A band's best of at least `PICTURE_MATCH` (0.45) places the corner (that map's frames scored 0.65-0.74, any other place 0.20-0.26). After a whole search finds nothing the next waits `PICTURE_RETRY_S` (1 s). `shift()` is how far the corner is from `PICTURE_BASE` (47, 72), in whole game px times the stretch: subtract it from a dot to read it with the first map's origin.

**Geometry.** The constants were measured at 1920x1080; `sizes(geo)` converts them (areas by the stretch squared) for any client size.

modules.title: Her name tag
modules.tagline: Finds her on screen by her name tag, near where she was first.
modules.summary: `NameTag.find` matches her name tag's full-resolution gray template on each frame and returns its centre in look-frame px. It searches near where she was found last first, then the whole play area, and picks the match nearest her last place because her name also shows in the minimap, the bottom bar and the party list.
modules.details_md:
Her tag is matched in gray with `TM_CCOEFF_NORMED` on the **full-size** frame: at half size the score swings between about 0.6 and 0.9 depending on which pixels the downscale keeps, and her name in the minimap scored about 0.6 too.

**The template.** Calibration keeps a half-size template (`small`). On the first look `_cut` finds her with it on all four ways of halving the frame (pixel offsets 0 or 1 across and down), needs `CUT_MATCH` (0.75), and cuts the full-size template exactly where it matched, so a name next to hers can't get in; it is saved per client size (`lab/tag_template_full_1366x768.npy`, `lab/tag_template_full.npy` at 1920x1080; another character's under `lab/characters/<her files>/`). If she isn't found it raises `RuntimeError` ("run `calibrate --fresh`"), which Eyes turns into a `tag` problem. After `RECUT_AFTER` (50) finds in a row without her, the template is cut again in case it no longer matches her (in the 2026-10-24 tours, 7,646 looks, her tag was hidden 14 looks in a row at most); if calibration's template doesn't find her either, nothing changes.

**Where it looks** (`find`). The camera keeps her at one spot on screen except near the map's edges, so a find searches within `NEAR_FRAME` (80 x 40 px, about a frame's move) of where she was first, then within `NEAR` (240 x 120), then the whole play area (above `PLAY_BOTTOM`, 0.9 of the height). Every `FULL_EVERY`-th (30th) find searches the whole play area anyway, so a wrong match can't stick (the code's comment reckons 1 s at the service's 30 frames a second of then; at its 15 a second since 2026-10-30 that is about 2 s; 150 was tried on 2026-10-26 and gave 30 s between hunts). Costs: 1.6 ms near, 3.6 within NEAR, about 35 ms for the whole play area, which `_banded` splits into `BANDS` (4) row bands on a thread pool (OpenCV lets go of Python's lock): 12.5 ms against 24.3, the same answers.

**Which match is hers** (`search`). Matches in the minimap corner are ruled out (`MINIMAP_WIDTH` 0.17 x `MINIMAP_HEIGHT` 0.3 of the screen). Up to `CANDIDATES` (4) matches of at least `MATCH` (0.7) are compared, each blanking `SAME_NAME` (20 rows x 60 columns) around it, and the one nearest where she was found last wins (before she's been found, nearest the screen's middle at `START_HEIGHT`, 0.6 of the way down). The answer is the tag's centre in look-frame px.

`lose()` forgets where she was (after a look that failed its checks), so the next find searches everywhere. Since 2026-10-30 the perception service can place her by the scene instead (localization.locate's Locator: this gray template first, then `plate`, then `poses`).

modules.title: Her name plate
modules.tagline: Finds her plate by its exact colours, even half covered.
modules.summary: Since 2026-10-29 her tag is a plate item the game draws bit-exact, so where the gray template isn't sure, counting the plate's stable pixels in their exact colours still finds it: whatever covers part of it only takes pixels away. Her name's white letters tell her plate from another wearer's. Used by the scene locator (localization/locate.py); the model is built at calibration (localization/her_cues.py).
modules.details_md:
Her tag is an orange-ribbon **plate item** (a wood frame, a mushroom icon left, a maple leaf right, her name in white on a translucent dark interior), drawn bit-exact: 99.9% of its stable pixels (1,395 of its 114 x 33 box, in 40 colours) equal its model in 60 sure frames. Ported on 2026-10-29 from the localization prototype, which found her this way on 77 of 81 hard frames where NameTag found 12%. Its counting is in C (`gamelab/locate.c`'s `lc_plate`, 32 places a step on AVX2; 0.2-0.4 ms for a window around a prediction), numpy otherwise, the same candidates to the integer.

**The model** (`PlateModel`, built at calibration by `PlateModel.build` from frames where her tag is sure): the median picture of the `BOX` around her tag's centre and each pixel's share of frames within `SAME_COLOUR` (12) of it; pixels with share of at least `STABLE_SHARE` (0.9) are stable. Of those, her name's **letters** (pure white inside `INTERIOR`) are hers alone; the **frame** pixels (less the pure black outline, which is everywhere) are shared by anyone wearing the same plate item (another player's matched 998 of its 1,252 frame px); white in the interior's background is someone else's letters (**bad**). `FEET` (1.5, -16) is her feet from the plate's centre.

**Candidates** (`Plate.candidates`). At every position of a window, count the stable pixels whose exact 24-bit colour the frame has there (frame pixels mapped to the plate's palette by a multiplicative hash, `_palette_hash`). Take the `TOPK` (3) best over `FLOOR` (40), at least `SUPPRESS` (3 rows, 5 columns) apart; refine the first by ±1 px on its evidence (frame + `W_LETTERS` 4 x letters - 2 x bad); and count `clean` letters: her letters in 8 px column bins (`BIN_WIDTH`) that show at least 85% of theirs with at most 1 stray white.

**The decision** (`Plate.decide`, the rules in `DEFAULTS`). A candidate needs `clean_min` (16) clean letters (another wearer's plate showed 8 at most; hers 52 or more on all but 6 of 2,089 frames), then the letters' rule (frame px at least 150 and letters - 0.5 x bad at least 15), or near a prediction the near rule (frame px at least 280, within 8 x (1 + frames unplaced) px, letters - 0.5 x bad at least -10), or with no prediction the far rule (letters - 1.0 x bad at least 25). The best by score less `W_DIST` (2) a px from the prediction wins if it is `aligned` (its count at least 0.97 of the best count within 12 x 6 px): another wearer's plate whose name shares letters with hers lines up its letters there, not its frame.

**Entry points.** `near(frame, pred, miss)` searches `NEAR` (60 x 40 px) around a predicted centre, `GROW` (25 x 15) wider for each frame she went unplaced, up to `GROW_MAX` (4); `verify(frame, peaks)` checks the gray template's first three peaks anywhere with the far rule. The gray stage (`gray_best`, `gray_near`, `gray_peaks`) is NameTag's template matched down to the HUD's top (row 700, past NameTag's 691: 4 hard frames had her plate there), the whole play area in 4 row bands on threads.

**Calibration helpers.** `sure_levels` sets the template's typical, picks and bank levels from its own score distribution (typical = 75th percentile; picks and bank 4 and 8 spreads below, capped at 0.95 and 0.9); `sure_centres` / `pick_centres` choose up to 400 sure frames spread over a 6 px grid; `tag_template` cuts a new gray template from the model's stable letters (BugBaby's scored 0.993 median against the old template's 0.879); `recentred` moves the model to that template's centre; `axis` is her mirror axis from the plate's stable columns.

modules.title: Her body by her poses
modules.tagline: Finds her body pixel by pixel from a bank of her own poses.
modules.summary: Where neither her gray tag nor her plate places her, her body does: a bank of her exact poses learned at calibration, searched by her anchors (her glasses, the top of her rope pose) or by her colours' mass against the map's art, each candidate's pixels checked in C. Used by the scene locator (localization/locate.py).
modules.details_md:
Ported on 2026-10-29 from the localization prototype, which placed her by her body on every held-out frame where her plate didn't show enough, but took 7-80 ms of Python a search: too slow for the service's loop, then 30 frames a second. The pixel checks are in C (`locate.c`'s `lc_pack`, `lc_agree`, `lc_mass`), numpy otherwise, the same shares to the bit.

**The bank** (`PoseBank`, built at calibration by `build_bank` from frames where her tag is sure, with the camera's view of each and the map's art behind her, `Background`): each `Pose` is her pixels (her own colours only) at offsets from her feet, how often and at how many places it was seen, whether she stood on a platform's line in it, which way she faces, plus mirrored copies for the other facing. `Anchor`s are small parts drawn the same in nearly every pose: her glasses (found by their blue lenses, `LENS`) and the top `ANCHOR_ROWS` (20) of her commonest narrow pose off the ground (her back on a rope), each as drawn and mirrored (`place_anchors`). Tree Dungeon's bank had 98 poses, 36 mirrored.

**The search** (`BodyFinder.find(frame, box, view, pred, slack)`) over a window around the box her feet may be in:

1. *Anchors* (`anchor_hits`): each anchor's masked squared gray difference computed from two plain correlations, as drawn and as the blink after a touch darkens her (x 2), the best `HEAD_PLACES` (2) under `HEAD_SQ` (400, RMS 20); every pose holding that anchor is tried where the anchor puts her feet. If the best verified candidate agrees at least `HEAD_OK` (0.8), it's her.
2. *Mass*: else a picture of the window scoring +1 where her colours (a 64-level lookup as drawn and as darkened, `LUT_GAINS`) are in the foreground (more than `FG` 12 from the map's art), -0.5 other foreground, 0 on the art (without art: +1 hers, -0.25 the rest) is correlated with three lean groups' mean masks (upright, leaning left, leaning right: `LEAN` 9 px); the best `CENTRES` (3) places, every pose within `FINE_R` (3) px scored on `SCAN` (48) pixels, the best 24 verified.

**Agreement** (`_verify`): each candidate's `SUBSET` (160 pixels, seeded by its id) at ±1 px, then the best `VERIFY` (8) with all their pixels. A pixel agrees within `TOL` (8) on every channel, or within `DARK_TOL` (2) of half its colour (the blink). Pixels behind the HUD (row 700 down) are hidden, not missing: the share counts those above it, at least `SHOWN_LEAST` (0.5) of them (counted against her, BugBaby falling behind the HUD on held-out frames of 2026-10-30 was placed 29.5-33.8 px off for 4 frames). With a prediction, `MOTION_W` (0.015) of agreement is lost per px of jump beyond the slack (a cast draws one picture at two origins 25 px apart).

`tracked_box` gives the box and slack for a tracked search from the filter's spread; `mirror_axis` checks her mirror axis by her poses seen facing both ways (it agreed with the plate's own axis).

modules.title: Ground and ropes
modules.tagline: How far the ground under her goes, and ropes and ladders on screen.
modules.summary: `ground_extent` scans outward from her feet along the rows just below them until sky or sea shows; `find_ropes` finds long, thin, vertical runs of rope colour, only in the screen columns where the map's ropes can show. Localization uses both to pin down her place.
modules.details_md:
**The ground under her** (`ground_extent`, look-frame px). From her x outwards along the rows just under her feet (`GROUND_ROWS`, 2-7 half-size px below), a column is open air where more than half its pixels are sky (blue at least 30 over red and at least green - 20) or near white (all channels over 190); `OPEN_RUN` (3) open columns in a row end the ground. Dirt walls count as ground, so on a floor between cliffs it reaches the walls; on a floating platform it stops at the edges.

**Ropes and ladders** (`find_ropes`, full-size px). In the top `ROPE_ROWS` (90%) of the screen and only in the x ranges Senses hands over (`Eyes.rope_columns`, where the map's ropes can show; overlapping ranges joined by `_spans`), pixels of a rope strand's greyish beige are found with OpenCV (`_rope_pixels`: `ROPE_RGB` ranges, red 20-70 over blue, red and green within 30; 6 ms over the screen against 16 with numpy, the same pixels). Each strip is copied out first (OpenCV split a strip viewed in place 8 times slower), cut to the box around its rope-coloured pixels (`CROP_PAD`), closed 9 x 3 to join the twisted strands and opened 31 x 1 to keep tall thin shapes, then connected only in the box around what's left, starting on an even row and column (`_even`) so OpenCV labels exactly as on the whole strip. A shape is a rope when at least `MIN_ROPE_LENGTH` (90) px tall, at most `MAX_ROPE_WIDTH` (12) wide and on average at least `MIN_ROPE_FILL` (1.5) px wide. Pieces of one rope broken by something in front are merged (`ROPE_GAP`, 6 px across and 40 down). 4.2 ms a look against 31.4 for the whole screen before; the same ropes on all 31 saved 1920x1080 screenshots.

All px were measured on the 1920x1080 window and are converted by the frame's geometry (at 1366x768 a rope is drawn pixel for pixel, 1/1.40625 as wide).

modules.title: Her heading
modules.tagline: Which way she faces, from her own picture above her tag.
modules.summary: The game draws each pose facing left and mirrors it to face right, so her box above her name tag matched against her pictures as it is and mirrored tells which way she faces. Her pictures are her own, learned as she plays from looks whose keys leave no doubt, clustered into up to 8 pose pictures; a seed stands in until she has them.
modules.details_md:
**Reading** (`Heading.read`, through `Eyes.heading`). Her box above her tag's centre (`her_box`: `UP` 50 to `DOWN` 8 half-size px above, `HALF` 16 either side at 1920x1080; 71 to 11 up and 23 across at 1366x768), padded `PAD` (3) px, is matched with `TM_CCOEFF_NORMED` against her pictures as it is (she faces left) and mirrored (she faces right), the best of each over the pictures (`match`; the picture that matched best last is tried first, and one matching 0.4 and leading by `DECISIVE` 0.2 decides at once: 0.2 ms a read instead of 1.4). `decide`: the better way is hers if it leads by `SURE` (0.08) and matches at least `LOW` (0.3); else "close" or "low". Not read when the tag wasn't seen, her box is off the frame, or it reaches under the minimap, which the game draws over her (the only wrong reads on the old recordings).

A `Reading` is `strong` at a score of at least `ATTACK_SCORE` (0.4) and `ATTACK_MARGIN` (0.2) ahead: while her attack plays, control.actions goes by strong frames only, and a weak frame can add an arrow tap but never take one away (with pictures learnt from walks and jumps alone, 9 of 426 throw frames read the wrong way, none strong).

**Learning** (`learn`, from the hunter). A look whose keys say beyond doubt which way she faces adds its box turned to face left (`canonical`) to a pool of the newest `POOL` (300), one a second at most (`LEARN_EVERY_S`). With `FIRST` (6) boxes there's a first picture; every `REBUILD_EVERY` (30) new boxes `rebuild` runs k-means on a thread of its own (65 ms on a full pool at 1366x768) and keeps at most `REFERENCES` (8) cluster medians (one median picture left 15.9% of frames untold; eight, 1.4%). A look the pictures read the other way isn't learnt and counts against them: 12 of the last 20 (`OUTFIT`) means they aren't of her any more (a new outfit), and `forget` drops the pool.

**Files.** The pool and pictures are kept per window size (`lab/heading_1366x768.npz`, `lab/heading.npz` at 1920x1080) with the client size and box they're for, written to a `.part` file then `os.replace`d (a run cut off leaves the last whole one; on Windows the replace is refused while a reader holds the file, so the next save tries again). A file of another size or box, or unreadable, is set aside with a log line. Until she has pictures the seed stands in (`assets/heading_1366x768.npz`: 16 frames of her standing still, 4 pictures, her outfit of 2026-10-24).

**Measured** (2026-10-24): on the old 1920x1080 recordings, read with pictures learnt from the others, 1,232 of 1,249 frames told and every one right; at 1366x768, 20 frames of 5 scenes, 19 right (15 strongly), one not told, none wrong. About 0.2 ms a read at half size, about 1 ms at 1366x768.

modules.title: Her EXP number and the glyph reader
modules.tagline: Reads "13,549[67.02%]" exactly by drawing the game's own glyphs; never a wrong value.
modules.summary: Her EXP number is read glyph by glyph by drawing every glyph the game could draw at every position and finding the best path through the box exactly (dynamic programming), then demanding every cell fit clearly, the text follow the number's grammar, and the percent match a level's requirement. The same `Layout` machinery reads her HP number (hp_number.py) and her level (lv_number.py).
modules.details_md:
A wrong value must never come out; no value is fine.

**The model.** The game draws the status bar's number pictures (`gamedata.canvas.status_numbers`: the digits, comma, point and percent white, the brackets green, a digit 5 x 7 game px), each glyph its picture's width plus one blank column, the first with its top left at game px (749, 740) (`NUMBER_AT`: the bar's left, 279, plus StatusBar.img's posNumberExp, 470). On a 1920x1080 window the whole picture is stretched with bilinear filtering, game px (x, y)'s middle at screen ((x + 0.5) x 1920/1366 - 0.5, (y + 0.5) x 1080/768 - 0.5): `stretch_x` across, not 1.40625 (with 1.40625 the number came out 11 levels off on average, half a pixel to the right). At the game's own 1366x768 both are 1.

**Cells** (`cells_of`, cached per layout and geometry: 30 ms plus 150 to draw them all, once). Every glyph, and a blank game column, is drawn at every game x it could start at, over the box read (`read_box`: 139 x 16 px at 1920x1080, 99 x 12 at 1366x768; two rows of plain bar above the glyphs and three below). Glyphs never share a game column, so the box's screen columns split into cells of one glyph each, and a reading is a path of cells across the box.

**Reading** (`read_text`). The background is each row's darkest `BG_SHARE` (10%) of columns (the text only brightens a row), or, for a `panel` layout, the status panel's own picture (`panel_of`). Each cell's cost is its squared difference from the screen; dynamic programming finds the best path exactly (cost so far forward, cost to the end backward). Every cell of the best path must then be within `FIT` (4 levels RMS) of its glyph as drawn (0.68 at most on the saved frames), and every other path through its first column must be worse by `LEAD` (10 levels; the nearest on the saved frames was 14.1, a '[' against a ']').

**Grammar and the table** (`read`). The text must match `NUMBER` (digits with a comma every 3, then the percent with two decimals in brackets, then only blank cells: a digit-like cell after it means one was missed), and the percent must be what the EXP is of some level's requirement within `PERCENT_SLACK` (0.51 hundredths: the game rounds) using `maplehelper.ocr.exp_table.EXP_TO_NEXT` (Classic World's table). Under about 1% several levels fit; the reading lists them (`levels`), and `level` is set only when one fits.

**Cost and use.** 8.6 ms a reading (median, on the 17 bench frames at 1920x1080), done only when 3 or more of the number's text pixels change (`hud.exp_changed`), about once a kill. The world step (localization.worldstate) turns readings into `exp_gain` / `exp_read` events, and localization.gains names the kills a gain was. `draw` / `draw_text` draw a number with the reader's own model over the bar's colours (`BAR`) for the simulator.

**Measured**: all 32 saved 1920x1080 frames and 19 saved crops of the bar read right; over 11 other backgrounds no value came out wrong in 825 tries; with a cursor-coloured block on the box, none of 183 was read.

modules.title: Her HP number
modules.tagline: Reads "[624/840]" exactly, whenever its pixels change.
modules.summary: Her HP number in the bottom bar (her HP now and when full) is read with exp_number's glyph reader (the same glyphs plus a slash, the same exact path and FIT/LEAD checks) and the grammar [cur/max] with cur at most max. `Follow` reads it only when its box's pixels change. The safety stop measures her HP with it, and her max HP is read off it rather than taken from config.toml.
modules.details_md:
**Where.** StatusBar.img's posNumberHp (239, 45) from the bar's left (279) puts the first glyph's top left at game px (518, 740) (`NUMBER_AT`), on the same rows as the EXP number; its cells end before game x 610 (`NUMBER_END`: the "MP" label's outline is at 611). The box read is x 517-608, rows 738-749 at 1366x768 (`read_box`). Its columns sampling game x 517-518 are taken as background (`masked_to`): the HP label's "P" and its dark outline reach into them, and the '[' draws nothing there.

**Reading** (`read`). `exp_number.read_text` with the `HP` layout (glyphs `0123456789[]/`, '/' drawn with the 'slash' picture), then `FIT` (4) and `LEAD` (10), then the grammar `NUMBER` (`[cur/max]`, 1-5 digits each) and cur at most max. Any failure gives no value with why; a wrong value must never come out.

**Following** (`Follow`). The world step (localization.worldstate) hands it the HP box of every frame; it reads only when the box's pixels change (and at the first frame), keeping what it said in between (`now`, `of`). `see` returns the reading and the HP the number said before the change (None if that wasn't read, so a drop between them isn't exactly known); a frame with no box resets it (the world step also forgets it over a frame not read or 1 s without one: `worldstate.HP_GAP_S`). About 5.4 changes a minute hunting, 2.9 ms a read (median; 190 ms the first, making its cells, which `warm` does up front). The world step emits an `hp_read` event; behavior.safety keeps a reserve of touches in HP from it.

**Measured** (2026-10-28): of 40 lossless 1366x768 frames, 37 read (every cell within 0.58 of its glyph and 22.5 ahead of any other); the 3 refused have garbage bottom bars. Maxes read 752, 774, 796 and 840 at her levels 24, 25, 26 and 28. The rolling recorder's JPEG frames fail FIT on every frame (JPEG ringing), so the live reader relies on the service's lossless DXGI frames. The HP bar lags the number by 0.07-0.25 s after a change.

This module finds the window's panels by the game copy's pictures (or live templates), reads their value cells by OCR, and keeps a calibration of where the window opens. It sends no keys.
modules.details_md:
The user, 2026-10-28, on her DEF not being known at a first run: "You can open character stats panel to check the defense".

**The pictures.** The client's windows are the newer UI in the game copy's `UI/UI_000.wz`; the stat window is `CharacterStat.img`: the Main panel (185 x 281: name, job, level, HP, MP, EXP, fame, STR, DEX, INT, LUK, ability points) and, by its DETAIL button, the Detail panel (187 x 223: attack, W.DEF, magic, M.DEF, accuracy, evasion, crit rate and damage, speed, jump). Each value is drawn from its vector in a light cell (`LIGHT` (225, 223, 213)); `CELLS` were measured off the pictures (`cells_of`, checked by the tests).

**Finding a panel** (`find`). The panel's picture is matched with `TM_SQDIFF` under a mask leaving out what changes: the value cells, the DETAIL button, the AP box and AP buttons, and the Detail panel's left 4 columns (`DETAIL_LEFT`: its two backgrounds differ there). First within `SLACK` (4 px) of where it was last seen, else at half size over the whole frame and then to the px around the best place. The fit is levels squared a channel over the masked pixels: at most `FIND_FIT` (400) means it's there (0 for the picture pasted in, about 30 as a JPEG, 20,000 and more on a frame without it). `shown(frame, cal)` checks only the calibrated place, every 4th pixel (0.06-0.08 ms a panel against 6-13 ms for `find`): localization.locate uses it to know when the window covers her.

**Reading** (`read`). Each panel's value cells are grouped into columns (`_columns`), each column read by the shared OCR in one call (maplehelper.ocr's RapidOCR, enlarged x 2), each OCR row given to the cell its centre falls in, and `parse` turns text into values ("840 / 840" to (840, 840), "60 ~ 75" to (60, 75), "100%" to 100). A `StatReading` holds each panel's place, texts, values and why not.

**Calibration** (`Calibration`, `lab/stat_window.json`). When the reader was written no saved frame showed the window (it has been on live frames since: hunts' starts on 2026-10-29 and 10-30 kept `lab/shots/statwindow_*.png`, and `shown` was measured on a live clip of 2026-10-30), so a hunt opens it only once a live capture has calibrated the reader (`gamelab stats --read --record`): where each panel opened, whether Detail opened with Main, and whose pictures found it. If the copy's pictures don't match the live window, `calibrate` cuts live templates from the frame (the windows that opened, `changed_boxes` against a frame from before), finds their value cells by their OCR'd labels (`layout`, `LABELS`), and saves them under `lab/stat_window/`.

`read_wdef` is the older single-value read (`gamelab stats --frame`). `compose` draws the window from the copy's pictures with any values (tests, simulator), and `Drawn.ocr` stands in for the OCR by answering what it drew.

modules.summary: Reads the game's KEY BINDINGS window off a 1366x768 frame: which keys carry ATTACK, whether it's in the unbound tray, the preset in use, and whether the window is wholly in view and legible. `functions` maps every key to its function or her item and skill pictures. behavior.keycheck opens and closes the window; control.keymap follows what it says.
modules.details_md:
On 2026-10-28 the user had moved the regular attack off Ctrl in their own play and hadn't put it back; about 20 of the bot's presses did nothing, unnoticed. The user's chosen fix included "Open keyboard config (\\) to check the key configuration and see if attack button is different". This module reads that window: the newer **KEY BINDINGS** window, not the classic v83 KeyConfig (live it opened at (177, 174)-(813, 619)).

**The pictures** are the game copy's `UI/UI_000.wz` KeyBindings.img, cut into `assets/keybindings` by `cut_assets` (and her items' and skills' icons by `cut_pictures`). The game draws them as they are: on the live frame every one of the 43 function pictures on a key matched its own to the pixel (rms 0.0-0.07), the best other at 57.6.

**`Reader.read`** (20-25 ms a frame):

1. *The window*: its title strip (the background's top `TITLE_ROWS` 20 rows, 636 wide) matched over the frame, `TM_SQDIFF_NORMED` at most `TITLE_OK` (0.06; 0.0076 live, 0.38 after Esc) and the whole window inside the frame; else its left `TITLE_PART` (100) px alone at most `PART_OK` (0.02) means it's open but partly off the frame.
2. *Levels*: the crop's brightness brought back to the pictures' by a gain and offset fitted on the title strip (`_levels`), for a frame the game dims.
3. *The tab and gaps*: the Keyboard/Mouse tab drawn selected, and the keyboard's own pixels between key cells as drawn (`GAPS_OK` 0.9 within `GAP_LEVELS` 16), else "covered" or "the Controller tab".
4. *The preset*: the page button drawn "checked" (0.9, the others under 0.6).
5. *Every bound key cell* (`CELLS` from `ROWS`: 74 keys by config.toml's names): ATTACK's picture's bottom `ICON_ROWS` (16) rows (the key's name is drawn over the top) matched within `SLACK` (3) px, scored by the mean-removed RMS difference: at most `ATTACK_OK` (25) is ATTACK, over `ATTACK_UNSURE` (45) not, between unsure (keycheck then reads a second frame). An exact draw scores 0.0-2.4, a frame 30% dimmer 20.4.
6. *The tray*: ATTACK's picture in an unbound slot means the game has it on no key.
7. *Legibility*: each key's name drawn as it is (`LABEL_OK` 0.75 of its px); with ATTACK found nowhere and some keys illegible (a popup or pointer over them), the answer is "covered", not "on no key".

**`Reader.functions`** (about 0.5 s): every function picture at every cell (`FUNCTIONS` names them), and on a cell with some other picture, which of her items' and skills' pictures it is (`PICTURES`: Lucky Seven, Pet Food, The Green Relaxer, the magician's four; `PICTURE_OK` 0.8 of the opaque pixels drawn as they are, any wrong one 0.60 at most).

Both Ctrls (and both Shifts, both Alts) are one binding to the game, which binds by scan code (`SAME_KEY`, `same_key`). `compose` draws the window with any bindings (`LIVE` is the live window of 2026-10-28, preset 2) for tests and the simulator.

modules.tagline: The masked colour match the monster and loot detectors share, in C where possible.
modules.summary: One place for the masked, normalised colour match (only a template's opaque pixels count) and for keeping the best of overlapping detections. Where the C is built and the CPU has AVX2 the match runs there, exactly in integers and about four times OpenCV's speed; otherwise OpenCV's.
modules.details_md:
Used by `mobs.py`, `loot.py`, `deaths.py` and `sprites.py` (other slices for the first three).

**The match** (`masked_match`): OpenCV's `TM_CCOEFF_NORMED` with a mask, the score at every place of the image; where it is undefined (a flat window: NaN or infinity), -1. In C (`native.py`, `native.c`'s mm_* functions) it is worked out exactly in integers, within 1e-6 of OpenCV's own in colour and 3e-5 on brightness.

**Made ready once** (`prepared`): each (template, mask) pair's sums and the mask's runs are computed once, cached by the arrays' ids with weak references, so an entry goes when either array does (a reused id is told from its array by the reference). None without the C or AVX2.

**Many templates, one call** (`best_matches`): a few templates over one window (a monster re-found) are matched in a single C call, the image loaded once, stopping at the first whose best reaches `stop` (a re-found monster stops at its first picture scoring mobs' REFIND_GOOD); the rest only if the caller goes on. Templates the C won't take fall back to OpenCV one at a time.

**Measured** on 60 frames of a crowd (2026-10-26 01:01, one thread, best of 5): a re-find's window 0.45 ms against OpenCV's 1.57, a step-2 check 0.05 against 0.58, a drop's strip 0.28 against 0.68; about 4 times as fast over all, with the same best places and the same decisions at the 0.55, 0.6 and 0.9 thresholds on all 2,894 calls.

**`suppress_overlaps`** keeps, best score first, each detection that doesn't overlap one already kept (centres closer than half the larger width and height).

modules.title: The exact finder
modules.tagline: Finds monsters near her by their pictures' exact pixels, however little shows.
modules.summary: Beside the main masked search (mobs.py), the exact finder finds monsters partly covered by her body, pet, plate, damage numbers or drops: at the game's own size a monster's visible pixels are its picture's exactly, so rare pixel pairs vote for places and exact pixels are counted. Its finds are added only where the search has no detection; a die1 find marks a death seen.
modules.details_md:
**Why** (the user, 2026-11-04, watching the live grind: "mobs near the player are not detected by perception"). Nothing masks her region: her body, pet, plate, damage numbers, effects and drops cover parts of monsters, and the search's masked correlation falls with the share still showing. On a lossless clip of 2026-11-02 22:49 the search found a monster on her level on 6% of frames within 25 units across of her and 27% at 25-50; by share showing, 7% at 0.2-0.4 and 91% at 0.8-0.95. Lowering its thresholds found scenery before it found much more.

**The idea.** The game draws a picture's opaque pixels as they are: on a frame of its own size, neither scaled nor compressed, what shows of a monster is its picture's pixels exactly. Each picture's **anchors** (`anchors_of`: pairs of side-by-side opaque pixels of different colours, the pair at most `RARE` (3) times in the picture, the first pixel's colour bin at most `SPARSE` (100) px a frame on the map's background, using `gates.bins` and the background counts; thinned to about `MOST_ANCHORS` (300) spread over it) vote for the places they fall on the frame. A place with `MIN_VOTES` (6) votes has its pixels counted, and `MIN_EXACT` (200) exact pixels or more is a find (pictures are about 1,800-3,000 px on Tree Dungeon's mushrooms; at 200 or more, 1 of 192 had its kind flipped under 30% showing). Each frame pixel belongs to one find only. All in C (`exact.c`, `native.exact_lib`): the frame's other pixels stop at a colour table, about 3 ms a frame on one thread.

**Pictures** (`pictures_of`): the detector's templates that come from the game data (with an origin, not screenshot cut-outs) and the death watch's die1 frames, both facings.

**Beside the search** (`fresh`): a find is added only where no detection lies within `NEAR_PX` (8 px, feet to feet), as a detection of score 1 (exact pixels of a live picture, however little shows, which the death watch shouldn't doubt). A die1 find isn't added: it tells the world step that monster's death was seen, about at once instead of 1.4 s on. `confirmed` says whether the finder can see on these frames at all: it finds nothing on a fade-in, a shade, another size or a JPEG.

**Measured offline**: against an exact-pixel oracle on the 22:49 clip, 100% in every distance band (by the README's NEAR_SEEN measure on the world step's dumps, under 25 units the search alone had 38.3%, with the finder 100%); on 72 frames labelled blind, of 47 live, solid monsters the search found 32, with the finder 47. Not run live yet.

modules.title: Monster sprites as templates
modules.tagline: Builds monster templates from the game's sprites and makes the map's detector.
modules.summary: Writes each monster's frames from the game data as PNG templates at the size they appear on screen, with what the game data says of each frame (origin, body box, head, delay); matches the old screenshot cut-outs against them for their feet and facing; makes the map's `MobDetector` (`detector_for`); and measures a map's background colours for learned gates (`learn_background`).
modules.details_md:
**Two sizes** (`folder_for`). For the old 1920x1080 window, pictures are resized 1.40625 times linearly with their alpha cut at `mobs.OPAQUE` (128), in `gamedata/data/out/sprites`; for the game's own 1366x768 (stretch 1) they are the game's pictures exactly, alpha and all, in `sprites_x1` (`GAME_ALPHA` marks such an entry; pictures built before it are built again). `build` writes `<kind>_<action><index>.png` for every stand, move and hit frame (`gamedata.canvas.mob_frames`) and each frame's data into the folder's `index.json` (origin, lt, rb, head, delay, size); `ensure` builds only what's missing. They're extracted game data, so they're git-ignored.

**Screenshot cut-outs** (`gamelab/assets/mobs`, of the 1920x1080 window: good at monsters half hidden in plants) are matched once against their kind's sprites both ways (`cutout_origins`: the masked match, the cut-out padded `CUTOUT_PAD` 30 px); a best of at least `CUTOUT_SCORE` (0.85; the 11 cut-outs matched at 0.86-0.98, the wrong way round 0.29-0.52) keeps the sprite's feet and facing for the cut-out (`cutouts.json`). At 1366x768 cut-outs aren't used.

**The map's detector** (`detector_for(model, geo, background)`): the sprites of every monster that spawns on the map and has either a hand-made colour test (`mobs.PALETTES`) or a learned gate. At 1366x768 the detector holds the map's own kinds only, sprites alone, so what it looks for doesn't depend on what was built for other maps; at 1920x1080 the cut-outs too. Kinds without a hand-made test get gates learned from the map's background counts (`gates.load_background`); a map with none kept gets a detector that doesn't look for them.

**Background colours** (`learn_background`, `python -m gamelab learn-colours`): from saved frames of any size, the play area above the HUD at step 1's scale, with the monsters found on it cut out `CUT_PAD` (6) game px around, over `CUT_ROUNDS` (2) rounds: first with gates learned against the frames as they are, monsters and all, then against the background without the monsters found. Tree Dungeon's came from 20 frames (53 monsters cut out).

flows.title: From a screen frame to an Observation
flows.summary: How the perception service turns the screen into what's on it, 15 times a second: a checked frame, then Eyes.look_at's reads in order.
flows.trigger: The perception service's frame loop (localization/feed.py run), once a pass.

steps.text: The loop asks its frames for the next frame due (`runner.frames.next(due)`).
Finds the game window and checks it (`framecheck.window_problem`). A window not fit to read gives a not-visible Frame with its Problem; the loop recovers the eyes and waits.
The grabber's shot (DXGI, waiting up to 20 ms for a frame shown after `due`) is converted BGRA to RGB into a reused picture.
A window moved during the shot, a frame 2 s old, or the game drawing off its client make the frame unfit. A frame held over 0.5 s keeps its own time.
For a visible frame that is new (or that a client asked about) the world step calls the Look, which calls `Eyes.look_at(frame.full, frame.t, ropes)`; an unchanged frame nobody asked about is skipped.
HP and MP from one row of the bottom bar, read first (a refused frame keeps the last good ones).
The two anchors (minimap title strip, HUD border). A failure gives a refused Observation (`bad` set) and the loop calls Eyes.recover.
The map's minimap picture located, near its last place first; never found refuses the look as `picture`.
Her yellow dot (up to the picture's right edge) and other players' markers, shifted to the first map's origin.
Her tag's centre, near where she was first; or the scene locator's answer (gray tag, then plate.py, then poses.py).
The ground under her, and ropes in Senses' columns when asked (`find_ropes`).
The Observation: her tag, HP/MP, ground, dots, ropes, the EXP text pixels and the EXP/HP/level boxes, the minimap picture's place, the chat box. Localization places it on the map.

flows.title: When a look fails its checks
flows.summary: What happens to a frame that isn't of the game as expected: it's never acted on, the eyes recover what they can, and a command stands still if it lasts.
flows.trigger: A frame or its window fails a framecheck check.

steps.text: The window is checked first. A window of another size, minimized, gone or off screen (WAIT_KINDS) is waited out: a look asks the window alone (`Eyes.window_wait`) and never brings the game forward.
On the pixels: both anchors off means `find_offset` says how far (offset) or the border found far up (drawn); only the strip off is `minimap`; only the border `hud`.
The Observation carries `bad` (the Problem) and the last good HP and MP; nothing else is read from it.
The service's loop asks the eyes to recover, at most every RECOVER_EVERY_S (0.2 s).

The minimap picture, name tag and locator forget their last place. For CAPTURE_KINDS (offset, stale, capture): the duplication is reopened at the first failure, mss takes over for 10 s at the second, then the two in turn every 5 s.
The DXGI desktop duplication is made afresh (or `fall_back` hands over to mss).

A command's look with no state to act on is taken again RETRY_GAP_S (0.2 s) later; a size or drawn fault (FIX_KINDS) is handed to the window fix first (`_mend`: Alt+Enter twice, through the player); after LOST_S (3 s) without one, LookLost is raised.
After LookLost a hunt stands still, sending nothing, and looks again every PAUSE_POLL_S (0.5 s) until a look passes its checks or its time is up.

flows.title: Her EXP, HP and level numbers
flows.summary: How the bottom bar's numbers are read exactly, but only when their pixels change.
flows.trigger: Every frame the world step processes (localization/worldstate.py).

steps.text: Cuts her EXP number's text pixels (brighter than 150) and copies of the EXP, HP and level boxes into the Observation.
The world step's vitals pass looks at each new Observation's boxes.
3 or more of the EXP number's text pixels differ from the last frame: an EXP change.

On a change (or when the EXP meter wants a reading) the box is read: every glyph drawn at every place, the exact best path, FIT and LEAD per cell, the grammar, the percent against the level table. The step emits exp_gain or exp_read.
The dynamic programming over cells shared by all three numbers.

flows.summary: Which way she faces, off each look's frame, and how her pictures are learned from looks whose keys leave no doubt.
flows.trigger: After a look the hunter (behavior/hunter.py) asks Eyes.heading (not on a rope), hands the reading to control.actions (Actions.see) and, where her keys leave no doubt, teaches it (Eyes.learn_heading).

steps.text: Not told where her tag wasn't seen; her pictures for the window size are loaded on first use (lab's file, else the seed).
Cuts her box above her tag, padded 3 px; refused off the frame or under the minimap.
The box against up to 8 pictures as it is and mirrored, the last best first; a decisive lead stops early.
A lead of 0.08 and a score of 0.3 tell LEFT or RIGHT; else 'close' or 'low'.
A strong reading may go over her keys while she attacks; a weak one never makes a throw skip its arrow tap (Actions.faces: a weak frame can add a tap, never take one away).
A look whose keys leave no doubt adds its box (one a second, pool of 300); one the pictures read the other way counts toward OUTFIT (12 of 20 drop the pool).
Every 30 new boxes, k-means on a thread of its own makes up to 8 median pictures, saved via a .part file and os.replace.
